step_by_step_reasoning:
The architecture shows MX Player's video ingestion, transcoding, and content delivery pipeline.
1. **Ingestion & Pre-Transcoding**: Content teams ingest videos from a CMS into an EC2-hosted transcoding API. The API triggers a pre-transcoding Spot Fleet (Auto Scaling) to perform basic checks, audio, and subtitle transcoding, while sending messages to an SQS queue and initializing tracking tasks in ElastiCache.
2. **Transcoding**: The main Transcoding Spot Fleet (GPU/CPU instances in Auto Scaling) polls messages from SQS, fetches raw video files from S3, processes them (using advanced codecs like H.266/H.265/AV1), updates task completion status in ElastiCache, and writes transcoded media back to S3.
3. **Content Delivery**: End users stream transcoded video content via CloudFront, which caches and serves media assets directly from the S3 origin bucket.

graph.name: MX Player Video Transcoding and Streaming Architecture
graph.categories: Media & Entertainment, Compute, Storage & Content Delivery
graph.notes: MX Player handles over 200k hours of video and 300M+ MAUs using AWS Auto Scaling Spot Fleets (scaling up to 3,000 instances) to process ~100k videos in SQS queue within an hour while utilizing H.266 compression to halve bandwidth requirements.

nodes.name: SQS
nodes.notes: Holds task messages for video processing (handles 100k+ video queues)

nodes.name: ELASTICACHE
nodes.notes: In-memory cache for tracking task state and completion

nodes.name: TRANSCODING
nodes.notes: Large Spot Fleet (up to 3,000 GPU/CPU instances) executing multi-codec video transcoding (H.266, H.265, AV1)

nodes.name: S3
nodes.notes: Object storage holding raw input video and transcoded output media

nodes.name: CLOUD FRONT
nodes.notes: CDN serving cached media content to end users
